human_tolerance.notes: Nests in tree holes but 'may also use posts and birdhouses if sized and situated appropriately', and drums on trees or metal objects, so it turns up in built-up places with mature trees.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: 'breeding individuals exhibit intense site fidelity, with pairs consistently returning to the specific nest cavity they used in the previous year', and northern flickers are among the few woodpeckers that migrate; the southeastern yellow-shafted form is the form present in Alabama.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Judgement: the article says a mated pair needs one to two weeks to build the nest before the breeding season and that nestlings begin clinging to the cavity wall at about 17 days and fledge 25 to 28 days after hatching, but dates no season, so spring to early summer is authored.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: 'The northern flicker commonly breeds during the months of February to July, depending upon the temperature of the area.' One to two clutches per season, typically six to eight pure white glossy eggs, the second-largest of any North American woodpecker; incubation by both sexes for about 11 to 12 days; young fledge about 25 to 28 days after hatching.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: One to two weeks for a mated pair to build the nest. Both sexes excavate a cavity about 33-41 cm deep with an entrance roughly 5-10 cm wide, often facing east to south-east, lined only with a bed of wood chips; occasionally an old kingfisher or sand martin burrow is used.

phases.name: dispersal
phases.note: 'Those that do migrate tend to begin their spring migration towards the beginning of April and make their return between September and October.' Some southern populations are completely non-migratory.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: Those birds that migrate leave the northern breeding grounds from September and October and return from the beginning of April; the winter diet of the birds that stay shifts to berries and seeds, including poison ivy, dogwood, sumac and wild cherry.

vocalizations.description: A sustained laugh, ki ki ki ki, quite different from that of the pileated woodpecker. It is the only vocalisation the sources describe for the species, so it stands in for both the program's song and alarm slots.
A constant knocking, from drumming on trees or even metal objects, used to declare territory; woodpeckers sometimes choose metal because the aim is to make as loud a noise as possible.

'This bird's call is a sustained laugh, ki ki ki ki.' The male's mating call toward a female is described as 'woikawoikawoika', a call that 'drums and rattles' and rises into a loud noise; used toward another male the same call is a territorial signal.

'One may also hear a constant knocking as they often drum on trees or even metal objects to declare territory... the purpose is to make as loud a noise as possible, so woodpeckers sometimes drum on metal objects.' While drumming the bird spreads its wings and flashes its colourful tail underside.
A sustained laugh, ki ki ki ki, flat at first and then rising into a loud noise; several of these names derive from attempts to imitate it. Given on the ground, from a snag and in flight.
The same ki ki ki ki given as a territorial signal toward a rival, and a sharper version when a nestling or an adult is flushed from the cavity.

taxonomy.note: The former yellow-shafted and red-shafted flickers are treated here as one species, following the American Ornithologists' Union, which the article describes as the species problem.

external.note: iNaturalist, NCBI and eBird ids via Wikidata P3151, P685 and P3444.

common_names.note: The article adds yellowhammer, gaffer woodpecker, heigh-ho, wake-up, walk-up, wick-up, yarrup and gawker bird among more than a hundred traditional names.

range.note: Native to most of North America, parts of Central America, Cuba and the Cayman Islands; the southern yellow-shafted form C. a. auratus, the one present in Alabama, ranges from Florida to Virginia.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'flickers are the only woodpeckers that frequently feed on the ground', probing with the beak and flying up to trees to roost and drum.

traits.flight.note: 'Like many woodpeckers, its flight is undulating.'

traits.nest_type.note: 'The northern flicker generally nests in holes in trees like other woodpeckers', occasionally in old earthen burrows vacated by belted kingfishers or sand martins, and it prefers to excavate its own cavity.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of 86-167 g. The article notes the largest-bodied specimens are in the northern range and the smallest in Grand Cayman, so this is the full species range rather than the Alabama form.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'The oldest yet known "yellow-shafted" northern flicker lived to be at least 9 years 2 months old'; the red-shafted figure is 8 years 9 months. The yellow-shafted form is the one present in Alabama.

traits.diet.note: 'their primary food is insects. Ants alone can make up 45% of their diet', with flies, butterflies, moths, beetles and snails also taken; berries and seeds, 'especially in winter', including poison ivy, dogwood, sumac, wild cherry, grape and elderberry. The 65/20/15 split is judgement, keeping insects dominant as the article states.

traits.social.note: A mated pair builds and excavates the nest together, the male commonly incubating overnight and both parents incubating by day.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Judgement: the source describes daytime ground foraging, courtship calls and territorial drumming, and a nocturnal cavity roost, without labelling the pattern.

traits.defense.note: The article records only that flickers are sometimes driven from a nesting site by other cavity nesters such as the common starling, and that juvenile flickers are helpless against predators entering the nest; mapped to Flee on that basis.

traits.wariness.note: Approachable where mature trees and open ground exist: it forages in the open on lawns and uses posts and birdhouses, but it needs cavity sites.

habitat.use.note: 'flickers are the only woodpeckers that frequently feed on the ground'; the rest of its time is in trees, drumming and roosting.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Excavates and roosts in tree cavities, reusing and repairing damaged or abandoned nests.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights and their months follow traits.diet and the article's winter emphasis on fruit and seed; nest cavities and ground foraging in leaf litter and soil are from the diet and nesting sections.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'It is a cavity nester that typically nests in trees, but may also use posts and birdhouses if sized and situated appropriately', and it drums on metal objects.

seasonal.strategy.note: The species 'is one of the few woodpecker species that migrate', but pairs show intense site fidelity and return to the same cavity; the Alabama form is the sedentary southeastern yellow-shafted race, so ActiveYearRound is used.

seasonal.phases.note: Nest building one to two weeks before the breeding season, nestlings clinging to the cavity wall at about 17 days and fledging 25 to 28 days after hatching are described; the calendar window is authored because the article gives no dates.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'The young are fed by regurgitation and fledge about 25 to 28 days after hatching'; 27 days is the midpoint and the 0.8 scale is authored judgement.

look.note: Brown with black bars on back and wings, a black necklace-like patch on the upper breast, beige lower breast and belly with black spots, a dark tail above and a white rump conspicuous in flight; the southern yellow-shafted form is yellow under the wings and under the tail, which is where the accent colour is used. The rump, bib and wing bars are extra parts and the proportions are authored judgement.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program, the closest shared program for a woodpecker that perches, roosts in a cavity, drums and forages on the ground. food_tag invertebrate matches the ant-heavy diet. Both the song and alarm slots point at the species' single documented call, the ki-ki-ki-ki laugh, because the sources describe no separate alarm vocalisation; that is a wiring choice, not a claim that the call is an alarm call.

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis, perching) and locomotion modes: the species 'frequently feed[s] on the ground' by probing, climbs tree trunks to excavate and roost, and flies in the characteristic undulating woodpecker flight ('a quick succession of flaps followed by a pause'). Individual numeric and behavioural traits below carry their own entries.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. Invertebrate, fruit, berry and seed tags come from the Diet section; cavity from the nest excavation; perch from drumming, roosting and courtship on trees. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.

vocalizations.wheeko.note: Call and flight and Reproduction sections: 'This bird's call is a sustained laugh, ki ki ki ki'; 'The common sounds a male makes towards a female is woikawoikawoika... If the call is used towards a male, it is a territorial sign', and 'The call type is a chirp that drums and rattles'. It fills both the song and alarm slots because the source presents one call serving both functions.

vocalizations.drumming.note: Call and flight section: 'One may also hear a constant knocking as they often drum on trees or even metal objects to declare territory.' Cooldown is judgement.

seasonal.winter_fraction.note: Judgement: some northern-breeding birds withdraw south, but many winter well north of the breeding range, so roughly half the population stays.

vocalizations.laugh.note: 'This bird's call is a sustained laugh, ki ki ki ki'; 'the calls' pattern can be classified as flat and gradually rises into a loud noise.'

vocalizations.alarm.note: 'If the call is used towards a male, it is a territorial sign' and 'juvenile northern flickers are often helpless against predators who enter the nest'; the separate alarm call here is the same laugh used defensively, which is a judgement.
